## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Gicheva, Edmunds, Hutchins, Eilam, and Arshavsky (2026) is the best-scoped US descriptive evidence to date on how first-year college performance moved across the pandemic: near-universe linked K-12-to-college records for North Carolina's public four-year and community college systems (about 403,000 immediate enrollees from the high school classes of 2015–2022), identical outcome definitions in both sectors, and a horizon that reaches the 2022–23 academic year — well past the Spring-2020 window that bounds most prior work. Several facts it documents are robust and worth citing. The Spring 2020 jump in four-year completion (about +5 pp, +0.75 earned credits) was a grading-policy artifact, with pass-type grades rising from roughly 1.5% to over 11% of courses; community colleges show the mirror image, an 11 pp withdrawal spike offset by 9 pp fewer D/F grades, replicating Bulman and Fairlie's California finding in a second state. The deepest four-year declines arrived with the 2021 cohort (about −0.5 to −0.6 earned credits and −2 to −3 pp completion in 2021–22), not during the acute disruption, and aggregate completion was back near baseline by 2022–23. Fall-to-spring persistence fell 1.5–2 pp at four-year institutions (against a 95% baseline) and about 3.5 pp at community colleges for the 2020–21 cohorts. And relative gaps in successful completion widened for below-median-GPA students (the largest and clearest subgroup result, roughly 5–9 pp at four-year institutions) and by 2–4 pp for underrepresented-minority, economically disadvantaged, and female students. The paper's most quotable claim, however — that these declines "have persisted" and outcomes "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for those groups — is a claim about levels that no exhibit supports: Figure 4 plots only subgroup-minus-reference-group differences, the reference-group trajectories are never shown, and the aggregate series sit near zero at the last observation. All five sub-reviews converge on this point independently. Three further calibrations matter. The community-college decline is confounded with the RISE developmental-education reform (2019–2021), which moved weaker students into exactly the credit-bearing courses the analysis retains, and the last Spring 2023 community-college points are at or above baseline despite the text's "sustained" language. Spring-semester estimates condition on falling fall-to-spring persistence, so the visible fall/spring sawtooth and any "recovery" read off the right edge of the figures are partly survivorship. And inference for the four-year results rests on 16 clusters with no small-sample correction, while not one coefficient is reported numerically and there is no data-availability statement or code. The authors are candid that the design is descriptive — no untreated group, no separation from concurrent shocks — and that candor is the right frame. Cite the paper for the timing of the decline, the sector-mechanism contrast, and the widening relative gap by prior achievement; attach caveats to every "persistent decline" phrasing, to the female result, and to the community-college story as a pandemic effect; and obtain the Online Appendix (and ideally the coefficient tables from the authors) before building on specific magnitudes.

#### Key Strengths

- A rare data asset used at the right scale: course-level transcripts for the near-universe of North Carolina public high school graduates enrolling immediately in the 16-campus UNC System or the 58-college NCCCS (210,008 and 192,793 students), linked to NCDPI K-12 records for baseline GPA, economic disadvantage, English learner, and disability status — no survey nonresponse, both sectors on identical outcome definitions.
- A horizon no earlier US study could offer: extending through the class of 2022 lets the paper show that the deepest four-year declines came with the 2021 cohort, after the acute disruption, and that aggregate completion had returned near baseline by 2022–23 — the paper's most defensible novel finding.
- Outcome decomposition that reveals mechanism, not just magnitude: reporting attempted credits, earned credits, C-or-better share, and withdrawal/incomplete share side by side shows that four-year declines ran through D/F grades with flat withdrawals while community-college declines ran through withdrawals and rising part-time enrollment, and it diagnoses the Spring 2020 spikes as grading-policy incidence using footnote 4's pass-grade shares.
- Unusual candor about design limits and measurement threats: the Conclusion states plainly that the study is descriptive and cannot disentangle the pandemic from concurrent shocks; the text warns explicitly that a negative Figure 4 coefficient need not mean a subgroup declined; and the GPA scale/weighting changes, RISE, and the pass-grade surge are all disclosed.
- Numerical fidelity inside the Results: the magnitudes the prose states (0.75 credits, 5 pp, 11 pp, 9 pp, 1–2 pp persistence) verify against the figures, so the body text can be trusted where it sits next to its exhibit.

#### Key Concerns

- The headline subgroup claim is a level claim resting on relative coefficients: the abstract and introduction say declines "have persisted" and outcomes "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for URE, economically disadvantaged, low-GPA, and female students, but Figure 4 shows only differences from the reference group's change, the reference-group coefficients are never reported, and the aggregate series are near baseline at the end — the paper commits, in its most-read paragraphs, the exact inference error it warns against on page 10.
- The community-college story is confounded with RISE and overstated at the endpoint: the developmental-education exclusion interacts with a 2019–2021 reform that pushed weaker students into the retained credit-bearing courses, the main text offers no specification that holds course mix fixed, and the text's "sustained increase in course withdrawals" is contradicted by Figure 2c/2d's final Spring 2023 points at or above baseline.
- Sample selection and spring survivorship are unaddressed: enrollment fell differentially on exactly the margins studied (footnote 3), spring outcomes condition on fall-to-spring persistence that itself fell 1.5–3.5 pp, producing a visible fall/spring sawtooth; and because each cohort contributes one first year, "rebounded" means a later cohort did better, not that any affected student recovered.
- Inference and verification are thin: 16 four-year clusters with no small-sample correction, no pre-trend tests despite visibly sloped pre-periods in Figures 2a, 2b, 3b, and 3d, no multiplicity adjustment across roughly 200 reported coefficients, no coefficient tables, no data-availability statement or access pathway, no code, and a fall/spring outcome adjustment that underlies every main figure yet is specified only in an unavailable appendix.
- Positioning problems a reader may inherit: the novelty claim ("unlike other studies that focus on a single institution") is contradicted by the statewide and national studies the paper itself cites; the female result is uncontextualized and runs against the cited literature; grade-inflation, test-optional, and corequisite-remediation literatures bearing directly on the outcome and subgroup definitions are absent; and the reference list carries a wrong DOI (Rodríguez-Planas 2022b) and a misspelled author (Polikoff).

#### What to Rely On

- The Spring 2020 rise in four-year successful completion (about +5 pp) and earned credits (about +0.75) as grading-policy incidence, not improved learning — pass-type grades rose from roughly 1.5% to over 11% of courses and withdrawals stayed flat.
- The Spring 2020 community-college withdrawal/incomplete spike (about +11 pp) offset by fewer D/F grades (about −9 pp), aligned with the NCCCS emergency-grade guidance and replicating Bulman and Fairlie (2022) in a second state.
- The timing of the four-year decline: the largest drops in earned credits (about −0.5 to −0.6) and completion (about −2 to −3 pp) came with the 2021 high school cohort in 2021–22, after the acute disruption, with aggregate completion back near baseline for the 2022 cohort.
- The sector contrast in mechanism: four-year declines ran through D/F grades with essentially flat withdrawals; community-college declines ran through withdrawals and incompletes and through more students attending part-time.
- Fall-to-spring persistence fell about 1.5–2 pp at four-year institutions (against a 95% baseline) and about 3.5 pp at community colleges for the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, returning to trend for the class of 2022 at four-year institutions.
- Relative gaps in successful completion widened for students with below-median high school GPA — the largest and most robust subgroup finding (roughly 5–9 pp at four-year institutions in 2021–22, still around 5 pp at the end of the sample), and by 2–4 pp for URE, economically disadvantaged, and female students in the 2021 and 2022 cohorts — stated as widening gaps relative to the comparison group.
- Four-year summer enrollment rose about 5 pp from summer 2020 onward and stayed elevated — as a durable level shift in summer coursetaking, not as demonstrated credit recovery.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Declines have persisted" / "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for URE, economically disadvantaged, low-GPA, and female students — Figure 4 shows relative-to-reference-group differences only; the reference trajectories are unreported, so the level claim is reconstructed by the reader, not shown.
- The female-student finding as an established pattern — it is the smallest subgroup coefficient (about 2–3 pp, male-referenced), has no mechanism or literature behind it, runs against the cited evidence on male disadvantage, and may reflect the rising female share in the 2020–21 cohorts.
- The community-college decline as a pandemic effect — RISE moved weaker students into the credit-bearing courses the analysis retains over 2019–2021, no specification holds course mix fixed, and the final Spring 2023 completion and withdrawal points are at or above baseline.
- Any "recovery" read from spring semesters or from the right edge of the figures — spring samples condition on fall-to-spring persistence that fell during the pandemic, and later-cohort rebounds say nothing about the recovery of the cohorts that were hit.
- The below-median-GPA subgroup as a fixed preparation group — within-cohort rank neutralizes the documented scale and AP/IB weighting changes but not pandemic-era high school grade inflation or the UNC System's test-optional shift.
- The summer credit-recovery mechanism — explicitly untested (footnote 5), summer credits were flat conditional on enrolling, and the largest summer increase follows 2019–20, the year four-year credit earning rose.
- Specific magnitudes and the four-year confidence intervals — no coefficient is printed anywhere, 16 clusters with no small-sample correction make the four-year bands optimistic, and the fall/spring outcome adjustment underlying every figure is specified only in the Online Appendix.
- Any causal reading of the pandemic's effect — there is no untreated comparison group, and the authors state they cannot separate the pandemic from concurrent economic, policy, and political shocks.
- Generalization beyond first-year, immediately enrolling graduates of North Carolina public high schools at in-state public institutions — gap-year and delayed enrollees, private and out-of-state institutions, and outcomes past the first year are all excluded, and the abstract's "all ... high school graduates" overstates the sample.
- The paper's own novelty framing — do not repeat "unlike other studies that focus on a single institution"; Bird et al. (2022), Bulman and Fairlie (2022), and Howell et al. (2021, 2022) are multi-institution studies the paper itself cites. Cite it instead for the linked K-12-to-college records, the two-sector comparison, and the horizon through 2022–23.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides useful descriptive evidence on first-year academic progress among North Carolina public high school graduates entering the state's public universities and community colleges immediately after graduation. The displayed adjusted comparisons show an early university-sector improvement in recorded success, subsequent setbacks and later aggregate improvement, with community-college setbacks prominently involving withdrawals and incompletes (pp. 7–8, Figures 1–2). Less favorable later changes for female, underrepresented racial and ethnic, economically disadvantaged, and below-median-GPA students show why aggregate improvement should not be taken to imply equal recovery across groups (p. 10, Figure 4). My judgment is that its contribution lies in linked records, sector comparisons, and coverage of successive entering cohorts beyond the initial disruption. It establishes neither causal pandemic effects nor recovery of the same students over their college careers. Relative subgroup changes do not alone establish failure to regain each group's own baseline, and policy-dependent outcomes and changing enrollment selection further qualify the headline recovery claims. The weak reproducibility assessment concerns independent verification of exact estimates, rather than demonstrated computational error; the broad descriptive evidence remains usable, but precise magnitudes and stronger subgroup claims warrant verification before further reliance.

#### Key Strengths

- Linked school and college administrative records support transcript-based measures of attempted and successfully earned credits, course outcomes, and enrollment, with clearly stated population restrictions (pp. 3–5, Data Source, Sample, and Outcomes).
- Parallel sector displays separate credit accumulation, course completion, withdrawals, persistence, and summer participation, making the timing and form of academic difficulties visible rather than relying on GPA alone (pp. 7–9, Figures 1–3).
- The subgroup specification directly estimates differences in changes, and the paper explicitly explains their interpretation; Figure 4 provides useful evidence that aggregate improvement can coexist with unfavorable relative changes for particular groups (p. 6, Equation 2; p. 10, Figure 4).
- The literature discussion acknowledges divergent grade and persistence findings, while the conclusion recognizes the descriptive design. In my assessment, the extension across later cohorts and public sectors is a worthwhile empirical contribution within that literature (pp. 2–3, Background; p. 11, Conclusion).

#### Key Concerns

- Calendar-time comparisons cannot distinguish pandemic effects from other contemporaneous changes. Entrant composition varies across cohorts (p. 5, Table 1), and observed-covariate adjustment does not establish comparability in unobserved preparation or enrollment selection (p. 6, Equation 1; p. 11, Conclusion).
- The strongest recovery language exceeds what the main subgroup exhibit establishes: the introduction says outcomes 'have not recovered to their baseline levels' (p. 1), whereas the subgroup explanation says 'A negative coefficient estimate does not necessarily mean that the outcome decreased for the given subgroup' (p. 10, Figure 4 discussion). These are different contrasts, not proof of a numerical contradiction; unavailable subgroup appendices prevent checking the stronger absolute claim.
- Recorded success depends on grading and placement rules, including qualifying pass grades and exclusion of developmental courses during the RISE reform (pp. 4–5; p. 12, note 4). The text's 'share of courses' (p. 5, Outcomes) also differs from the plotted 'Share of credits' (pp. 7–8, Figures 1c–d and 2c–d; p. 10, Figure 4), leaving the weighting unresolved. These outcomes are not stable direct measures of learning.
- The supplied article identifies neither executable code nor an operational data-access route and incompletely specifies seasonal adjustment and analytic-file construction (pp. 3–6, 11). Online Appendices A and B are not bound into the PDF and are unavailable here. This limits exact replication and checks of baseline levels and auxiliary subgroup findings; it does not establish that the unavailable materials are inadequate or that confidential student records should be public.
- Scope and novelty require restraint: the sample excludes delayed entrants and students outside the covered public systems and follows initial college outcomes (p. 4, Sample). The contrast 'Unlike other studies that focus on a single institution' is overbroad alongside the same page's description of 'a sample of Virginia Community College System students' (p. 3, Background). In my judgment, the paper extends an existing evidence base rather than establishing national generality or priority for system-wide evidence.

#### What to Rely On

- Adjusted changes in recorded first-year academic progress among the specified immediate public-college entrants: the administrative outcomes and displayed sector patterns support this bounded descriptive use (pp. 4–6; pp. 7–9, Figures 1–3).
- Aggregate setbacks followed by improvement in successful completion: the final spring estimates are near baseline in both sectors, so recovery statements should name the outcome and observation period rather than imply uninterrupted decline (pp. 7–8, Figures 1c and 2c–d).
- Less favorable later changes in completion for the displayed subgroups relative to their comparison groups: these are the contrasts directly defined and plotted, not subgroup outcome levels (p. 6, Equation 2; p. 10, Figure 4).
- Increased university summer participation and temporary reductions in university fall-to-spring persistence: the enrollment indicators support those descriptive claims, with persistence restricted to return within the same public sector (p. 5, Outcomes; p. 9, Figures 3a and 3c).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Causal claims about COVID-19, remote instruction, flexible grading, or advising: the design lacks an unexposed comparison and does not isolate these mechanisms (p. 6, Equation 1; p. 11, Conclusion).
- Claims that every focal subgroup remained below its own baseline, or that women had lower success levels than men: relative-change coefficients cannot establish either claim without subgroup levels or reference-group changes and joint uncertainty (p. 6, Equation 2; p. 10, Figure 4).
- Recovery of lost learning, eventual credentials, or the same individuals over time: the outcomes concern recorded progress during successive cohorts' initial college year, within a selected population (pp. 4–5, Sample and Outcomes).
- Exact completion, withdrawal, or D/F magnitudes and isolated significance claims: course-versus-credit weighting is unresolved, coefficient tables and full implementation details are unavailable, and no small-cluster or multiple-comparison adjustment is reported in the supplied text (pp. 5–6; pp. 7–10, Figures 1–4). Under exhaustive categories on a common denominator, the D/F share is the complement of successful and withdrawn/incomplete shares, not their difference as the wording on p. 5 suggests.
- Summer study as a demonstrated remedy for failed credits, or nonpersistence as departure from higher education: neither course replacement nor enrollment outside the same public sector is established by these measures (p. 5, Outcomes; p. 9, Figure 3).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods: the early university increases are approximately 0.75 successfully earned credits and 5 percentage points in completion; these are visual approximations, not recovered coefficients (p. 7, Figures 1b–c).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: the community-college changes of approximately −2 percentage points in completion and +11 points in withdrawals/incompletes imply approximately −9 points in D/F on a common exhaustive denominator; the figure agrees with the numerical narrative despite the erroneous verbal derivation on p. 5 (p. 8, Figures 2c–d and accompanying text).
- CONFIRMED — Writing versus an unqualified persistence-of-decline reading: the final spring completion and withdrawal/incomplete estimates are close to baseline (p. 8, Figures 2c–d); 'a sustained increase in course withdrawals' (p. 8) needs the endpoint qualification also recognized by 'Course completion rates appear to be rebounding' (p. 11).
- CONFIRMED — Methods, writing, and contribution: the subgroup exhibit estimates differences in changes, not absolute subgroup recovery; the unfavorable later point estimates support the narrower interpretation used here (p. 6, Equation 2; p. 10, Figure 4 and note).
- CONFIRMED — Methods and writing: 'share of courses' in the outcome definition (p. 5) differs from 'Share of credits' on the result axes (pp. 7–8, Figures 1c–d and 2c–d; p. 10, Figure 4); the paper does not resolve the implementation.
- CONFIRMED — Methods and contribution: cohort composition changes are visible in Table 1 (p. 5), and the Sample section restricts the population to immediate entrants with linked North Carolina public-school records (p. 4).
- CONFIRMED — Contribution: Figure 3c shows increased university summer enrollment (p. 9), while the Outcomes section explicitly states that replacement of previously unsuccessful courses is not tested (p. 5).
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility and methods: exact seasonal-adjustment implementation, subgroup-specific baseline recovery, and appendix-only explanations cannot be verified from the supplied PDF; the cited online appendices are not bound into it (pp. 6, 9–11).
